stem: A 4-month-old girl had a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening. Her sweat chloride is 72 mmol/L on two occasions. A gene panel testing the 70 most common CFTR mutations finds a mutation on only one allele.
oneliner: 4-mo F + high IRT on newborn screen + sweat Cl 72 twice + CFTR panel: one mutation only → best explanation?
ask: Which of the following best explains these results?

options.A: The sweat test is a false positive
options.B: She has a second CFTR mutation not on the panel
options.C: She is only a carrier, so this is a different disease
options.D: A mutation in another gene that interacts with CFTR
options.E: The newborn screen was a false positive

whyNot.A: Sweat chloride **above 60 on two tests** is diagnostic
whyNot.C: Carriers have **normal sweat chloride**; this is cystic fibrosis
whyNot.D: CF is caused by **CFTR** mutations; panels miss rare CFTR variants
whyNot.E: The **sweat test confirms** the screen

answer: A second, rarer CFTR mutation the panel did not test (compound heterozygote)
why: CF is **autosomal recessive**: two faulty CFTR alleles are needed. **Two positive sweat tests prove the disease**, so the other allele must carry a **rare mutation** that the common-mutation panel missed (allelic heterogeneity).
chain: Two abnormal CFTR alleles (one common, one rare)
Panel finds only the common allele

idea.rule: A panel can only find what it looks for: many different mutations in one gene (allelic heterogeneity).
also: Same logic for BRCA panels and beta-thalassemia
Locus heterogeneity = same disease from different genes (e.g. albinism)

stem: A 5-day-old boy has a phenylalanine of 20 mg/dL on newborn screening. Sequencing of his phenylalanine hydroxylase gene is normal. At 4 months, despite a strict low-phenylalanine diet, he has hypotonia and seizures, and his cerebrospinal fluid has low dopamine and serotonin metabolites.
oneliner: 5-day M + Phe 20 + normal PAH gene sequence + hypotonia, seizures despite low-Phe diet + low CSF dopamine and serotonin metabolites → mechanism of high Phe?
ask: Which defect best explains his hyperphenylalaninemia?

options.B: Deficient tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase

whyNot.A: His **PAH gene is normal**; classic PKU would respond to the diet
whyNot.C: Tyrosine transport defects do not raise phenylalanine
whyNot.D: **Maple syrup urine disease**: raised leucine, isoleucine, valine
whyNot.E: **Alkaptonuria**: dark urine and ochronosis, phenylalanine normal

why: **Normal PAH gene plus high Phe** points to the **BH4 cofactor**. BH4 is also needed by **tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylase**, so **dopamine and serotonin fall** and neurologic disease continues despite the diet.
chain: Tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases also fail
Low dopamine and serotonin, neurologic damage

idea.rule: BH4 is a cofactor for PAH, tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase; BH4 defects mimic PKU but diet alone fails.
also: Treat with BH4, L-dopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan
Some PAH mutations respond to BH4 (sapropterin)
BH4 is also needed for nitric oxide synthase

stem: A 3-month-old girl with phenylketonuria is on a phenylalanine-restricted formula. Her plasma phenylalanine is now in the target range, but her hair and skin are lighter than her siblings', and another plasma amino acid that is normally made in her body is low.
oneliner: 3-mo F + PKU on low-Phe formula + Phe controlled + lighter hair and skin + another amino acid low → which must now be supplied?
ask: Which amino acid must now be supplied in her diet?

whyNot.A: Already essential for everyone; **not** made from phenylalanine (precursor of serotonin and niacin)
whyNot.B: Essential for all people; **ketogenic branched-chain** amino acid
whyNot.C: Essential for all; precursor of **cysteine** via homocysteine, not made from Phe
whyNot.E: Essential for all; purely **ketogenic**, not linked to phenylalanine

why: **Phenylalanine hydroxylase** converts **phenylalanine to tyrosine**. With the block, tyrosine can no longer be made, so it **must be given in the diet**; it is the precursor of **catecholamines and melanin**.

idea.rule: In PKU tyrosine is conditionally essential; fair skin and low catecholamines follow if it is not replaced.
also: Cysteine becomes essential in homocystinuria (cystathionine synthase deficiency)
Untreated PKU: musty odor, fair skin, intellectual disability
Maternal PKU: microcephaly, congenital heart disease

stem: A 34-year-old lean man (BMI 22 kg/m²) has LDL cholesterol of 280 mg/dL with normal triglycerides. His father had a myocardial infarction at 44. He has Achilles tendon thickening from xanthomas. He is not taking medication, and thyroid and liver tests are normal.
oneliner: 34M + lean + LDL 280, triglycerides normal + father MI at 44 + Achilles xanthomas + no drugs, normal thyroid and liver tests → mechanism of high LDL?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his raised LDL?

options.D: Reduced hepatic uptake of LDL through a defective receptor
options.E: Increased conversion of cholesterol to bile acids

whyNot.A: Would raise **triglycerides** (and be obesity-linked); his triglycerides are normal
whyNot.B: Would give a **mild** rise, not LDL 280 with xanthomas
whyNot.C: **Raises chylomicrons and triglycerides**, not isolated LDL
whyNot.E: **Lowers** cholesterol (drains it); it does not raise LDL

why: **Isolated LDL elevation with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease in a family** = **familial hypercholesterolemia**. A **defective LDL receptor** means the **liver clears LDL poorly**, so plasma LDL rises.

idea.rule: Isolated high LDL with early heart disease and tendon xanthomas means reduced LDL receptor clearance.
also: Heterozygotes: LDL ~300; homozygotes: LDL >600 and childhood MI
Other causes: ApoB-100 defect, PCSK9 gain of function
Treat with statins; PCSK9 inhibitors

stem: A 3-day-old boy is lethargic, vomiting, and feeding poorly. Ammonia is 650 µmol/L, blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, plasma citrulline is raised, and urine contains a large amount of argininosuccinate. Urine orotic acid is normal.
oneliner: 3-day M + lethargy, vomiting + ammonia 650 + respiratory alkalosis + high citrulline + large urine argininosuccinate + normal orotic acid → which step is blocked?
ask: Which enzymatic step is deficient?

options.A: Formation of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia
options.B: Cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate
options.C: Formation of citrulline from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate
options.D: Formation of argininosuccinate from citrulline and aspartate
options.E: Cleavage of arginine into ornithine and urea

whyNot.A: Would **lower citrulline**, not raise it, and give no argininosuccinate
whyNot.C: **OTC deficiency**: raised orotic acid and **low** citrulline; orotic acid is normal
whyNot.D: This step comes **before** argininosuccinate; its defect gives **high citrulline but no argininosuccinate** (citrullinemia)
whyNot.E: **Arginase deficiency**: high arginine, spastic diplegia, milder hyperammonemia

why: **Argininosuccinate piles up and spills into the urine**, so the block is **after it**: **argininosuccinate lyase**. **Ammonia cannot be converted to urea**, so it rises and drives respiratory alkalosis and lethargy.

idea.rule: The metabolite that accumulates marks the step just before the block; large urine argininosuccinate means the lyase step.
also: OTC deficiency: high orotic acid, low citrulline, X-linked
Citrullinemia: very high citrulline, no argininosuccinate
Treat with protein restriction, arginine and nitrogen scavengers

stem: A newborn girl has bilateral absence of the irises. Her father also has aniridia. Sequencing of the PAX6 coding region and splice sites is normal in both. Microarray shows no deletion. Karyotyping shows a balanced translocation between chromosome 11 and another chromosome in both, with the chromosome 11 breakpoint just downstream of PAX6. She has no Wilms tumor or genital anomalies.
oneliner: Newborn F + bilateral aniridia + father affected + normal PAX6 coding and splice sequence + no deletion on microarray + balanced 11 translocation, breakpoint just downstream of PAX6 in both + no Wilms, no genital anomaly → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the aniridia?

options.A: A nonsense mutation creating a premature stop codon in PAX6
options.B: Deletion of PAX6 together with neighboring genes
options.C: Skipping of an exon from a splice-site mutation
options.D: Separation of PAX6 from its regulatory sequences by the translocation breakpoint
options.E: Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat in PAX6

whyNot.A: **PAX6 coding sequence is normal**
whyNot.B: **WAGR** needs a deletion (none on microarray) and would give Wilms tumor and genital anomalies
whyNot.C: **Splice sites are normal** on sequencing
whyNot.E: No repeat expansion is described and **inheritance is dominant, without anticipation**

answer: Position effect: translocation separates PAX6 from its enhancers
why: **A normal PAX6 gene but a breakpoint just beyond it** means the **distant regulatory (enhancer) sequences** are separated. PAX6 **expression falls** (haploinsufficiency) even though the gene is intact; this is a **position effect**.

idea.rule: A translocation can cause disease without touching the coding sequence, by moving a gene away from its regulators.
also: WAGR: 11p13 deletion (Wilms, aniridia, genital anomalies, retardation)
PAX6 is a transcription factor for eye development
Balanced carriers are often healthy; translocations near a gene can still cause dominant disease

stem: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He has normal male external genitalia and small, firm testes, and semen analysis shows no sperm. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no uterus. Karyotype is 46,XX.
oneliner: 26M + infertility + normal male genitalia, small firm testes + no uterus + karyotype 46,XX → why testes?
ask: Which of the following best explains the development of his testes?

options.A: Translocation of the SRY gene to another chromosome
options.D: Nondisjunction giving an extra X chromosome

whyNot.B: **Androgen insensitivity** is 46,XY with female-appearing genitalia
whyNot.C: **Adrenogenital syndrome** virilizes a 46,XX baby but gives **ovaries and a uterus**
whyNot.D: **Klinefelter** is **47,XXY**; his karyotype is **46,XX**
whyNot.E: Causes **external** virilization of a female fetus, **not testes**

why: The **SRY gene** (testis-determining factor) normally lies on the Y chromosome. If it **crosses onto an X or autosome** during paternal meiosis, the 46,XX fetus makes **Sertoli and Leydig cells**, so it develops **testes** and a male phenotype.
chain: SRY crosses to X or autosome in meiosis
Testes form, with Sertoli cells (AMH) and Leydig cells (testosterone)

idea.rule: The testis is determined by SRY, not by the karyotype.
also: 46,XX males lack the AZF region, so they are infertile
46,XY females: SRY deletion (Swyer syndrome)
True hermaphroditism has both testicular and ovarian tissue

stem: A 5-month-old boy has lost motor skills he had gained. He is hypotonic with nystagmus and brisk reflexes, and his serum lactate is elevated. MRI shows bilateral basal ganglia lesions. A muscle biopsy shows markedly reduced succinate dehydrogenase activity.
oneliner: 5-month-old boy + developmental regression + hypotonia + nystagmus + raised lactate + basal ganglia lesions + low succinate dehydrogenase → which step is impaired?
ask: Which of the following reactions is most directly impaired?

options.A: Transfer of electrons from NADH to ubiquinone
options.B: Oxidation of succinate to fumarate with electron transfer to ubiquinone
options.C: Transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen
options.D: Use of the proton gradient to make ATP

whyNot.A: That is **complex I**, not succinate dehydrogenase
whyNot.C: That is **complex IV** (cytochrome c oxidase)
whyNot.D: That is **complex V**, ATP synthase
whyNot.E: **Lactate dehydrogenase** works in the cytoplasm; lactate is a **consequence** here

answer: Complex II converts succinate to fumarate and feeds electrons to CoQ
why: Succinate dehydrogenase is **complex II** of the electron transport chain and also an enzyme of the **TCA cycle**. It **oxidizes succinate to fumarate** and passes electrons to **ubiquinone** (CoQ). Loss causes **energy failure in the brain** (Leigh syndrome) and **lactic acidosis**.
chain: Electron flow and ATP production fall

idea.rule: Complex II is the only ETC complex that is also a TCA cycle enzyme and does not pump protons.
also: Complex I: NADH → CoQ; III: CoQ → cytochrome c; IV: reduces O2 to water
Leigh syndrome is a mitochondrial disorder (often maternal or nuclear inheritance)
Mitochondrial disease: lactic acidosis, high-energy organs affected

stem: A family has a fully penetrant autosomal dominant adult-onset disorder. A rare allele of a marker very close to the disease gene is present in almost all affected members, but two affected relatives lack it.
oneliner: Family + fully penetrant AD disorder + rare marker allele tightly linked + almost all affected carry it but two affected do not → what separated them?
ask: Which process most likely explains the two marker-negative affected relatives?

options.D: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the marker

whyNot.A: Would **not** specifically separate two linked alleles in only a few people
whyNot.B: Marker and gene lie on the **same chromosome** and are tightly linked
whyNot.D: A SNP is itself a marker; it does not **uncouple** alleles on one chromosome
whyNot.E: A **bacterial** gene-transfer process

answer: Meiotic recombination (crossing over) between the disease allele and the marker
why: Linked loci travel together, but a **crossover in prophase I** can swap the segment between them. The affected person then carries the disease allele on a chromosome with the **other marker allele**. The **closer the loci, the rarer the recombination**.
chain: Disease and marker allele on one chromosome

idea.rule: Exceptions to linkage are produced by recombination; the closer the loci, the fewer the exceptions.
also: Recombination frequency 1% = 1 centimorgan
Unlinked loci assort independently (50% recombinant)
Marker-disease association can differ between families

stem: A 4-year-old boy has Leigh syndrome from an A-to-G point mutation in a mitochondrial tRNA gene for leucine. A researcher asks why mitochondria encode their own tRNAs instead of using the nuclear-encoded tRNAs of the cytosol.
oneliner: 4M + Leigh syndrome + A→G mutation in mitochondrial tRNA-Leu → why does mtDNA need its own tRNA genes?
ask: Which feature best explains why mitochondria need their own tRNAs?

options.A: Matrix pH is too high for cytosolic tRNA to keep its fold
options.B: Reactive oxygen species would destroy any imported tRNA
options.C: Cytosolic tRNAs carry different amino acids from those mitochondria use
options.D: Cytosolic tRNAs lack the 3' CCA end needed for charging
options.E: Mitochondria use a modified genetic code that cytosolic tRNAs would misread

whyNot.A: Matrix pH is only mildly alkaline; tRNAs are **stable** there
whyNot.B: ROS damage mtDNA, but this is **not why** the genome carries tRNA genes
whyNot.C: Both use the **same 20 amino acids**
whyNot.D: All tRNAs have a **CCA end**

answer: Mitochondria use a nonstandard code (for example UGA = Trp, AUA = Met), so they need their own tRNAs
why: The **mitochondrial genetic code differs** from the universal one: **UGA codes for tryptophan, AUA for methionine**, and AGA/AGG are stops. Cytosolic tRNAs would **mistranslate** mitochondrial mRNAs, so mtDNA encodes **22 tRNAs** itself.
chain: Mitochondrial code differs from the cytosolic code
Cytosolic tRNAs would misread mitochondrial codons
mtDNA carries its own 22 tRNA genes
A mutation there stops respiratory chain synthesis

idea.rule: mtDNA is a self-contained translation system with a variant genetic code.
also: mtDNA encodes 13 proteins, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs
Inheritance is maternal with heteroplasmy
MELAS, MERRF, Leigh syndrome, LHON

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had repeated sinus and lung infections since infancy, finger clubbing, and a sweat chloride of 95 mmol/L. His older brother has the same illness. Genetic testing shows both copies carry a deletion of a single phenylalanine codon, and almost no CFTR protein is found at the apical cell surface.
oneliner: 6M + recurrent sinopulmonary infections + clubbing + sweat Cl 95 + affected brother + homozygous Phe deletion + no CFTR at apical surface → molecular defect?
ask: Which defect most likely accounts for the loss of channel function?

options.A: Overactive channel that cannot be switched off
options.B: Premature stop codon so no protein is made
options.C: Splicing defect giving a reduced amount of normal channel
options.D: Channel reaches the surface but fails to open
options.E: Misfolded channel retained in the ER and degraded

whyNot.A: Would cause **excess** chloride secretion, the opposite of this disease
whyNot.B: Her mutation is an **in-frame deletion of one codon**, so a full-length protein is made
whyNot.C: The change is a **codon deletion in the coding sequence**, not a splice-site change, and the protein made is abnormal
whyNot.D: That is a **gating** mutation (G551D); here **no protein reaches** the surface

answer: Protein-folding defect: mutant CFTR (delta F508) is degraded before reaching the membrane
why: **Phe508 deletion** makes CFTR **misfold**; the ER quality-control system **sends it for proteasomal degradation**, so **little chloride channel reaches the apical membrane**. Chloride and water secretion fall and secretions become thick; sweat chloride is high because the duct cannot reabsorb it.
chain: Thick secretions, infections, high sweat chloride

idea.rule: Some genetic diseases are trafficking defects: the protein is made but never reaches where it works.
also: Class I to VI CFTR mutations differ in mechanism
Correctors and potentiators target folding and gating
Sweat chloride high because duct cannot reabsorb Cl-

stem: A 5-year-old boy has had 6 fractures after minor falls. A deep cut on his knee healed slowly with a thin, weak scar. A photograph of his eyes is shown.
oneliner: 5M + 6 fractures from minor falls + deep cut healed slowly with a thin weak scar + eye photo shown → which part of wound healing fails?
ask: Which part of wound healing is most affected?

options.A: Migration of keratinocytes across the wound
options.B: Formation of the initial fibrin clot
options.D: Formation of the mature scar from type I collagen

whyNot.A: Not dependent on **type I collagen structure**
whyNot.B: Depends on **platelets and clotting factors**, normal here
whyNot.C: Depends on **chemotaxis**, not collagen
whyNot.E: Granulation tissue is mostly **type III collagen**, which is normal here

answer: Defective type I collagen weakens scar maturation (osteogenesis imperfecta)
why: **Blue sclerae and recurrent fractures** suggest **osteogenesis imperfecta**, a **type I collagen** defect (COL1A1/COL1A2). **Mature scars are mostly type I collagen**, so remodeling gives a **thin, weak scar**.
chain: Too little or abnormal type I collagen
Granulation-tissue type III collagen cannot be replaced by strong type I
Weak mature scar and fragile bone

idea.rule: A type I collagen disease affects bone, sclerae, skin and scars.
also: Blue sclerae: thin collagen lets the choroid show
Hearing loss from ossicle damage
Dentinogenesis imperfecta: opalescent, fragile teeth

image.prompt: Close-up of a young boy's eyes and upper face, eyes wide open: the whites of both eyes are obviously and strongly slate-blue in colour across the whole sclera

stem: A 78-year-old man lives alone and eats mostly tea and toast. He has lost 10 kg, looks wasted, and has bilateral pitting leg edema. Serum albumin is 2.5 g/dL, urinalysis shows no protein, liver tests are normal, and his jugular venous pressure is normal.
oneliner: 78M + lives alone, tea and toast diet + 10 kg weight loss + wasted + bilateral pitting leg edema + albumin 2.5 + no proteinuria + normal liver tests and JVP → mechanism of edema?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his edema?

options.A: Primary renal sodium retention from nephritic disease
options.B: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure from heart failure

whyNot.A: **No proteinuria** on urinalysis, and nothing points to a nephritic process
whyNot.B: **JVP is normal**
whyNot.C: Edema is **bilateral with low albumin**, not regional
whyNot.D: Leaky capillaries do not explain **low albumin from poor intake**; no burn or inflammation is described

answer: Protein malnutrition causing hypoalbuminemia and low oncotic pressure
why: **Poor protein intake** gives **negative nitrogen balance and low albumin**. **Albumin provides most plasma oncotic pressure**, so when it falls fluid moves into interstitium as **pitting edema**. No proteinuria and **normal liver tests** exclude other causes of low albumin.

idea.rule: Starling forces: lower oncotic pressure pulls less fluid back into vessels, so it accumulates.
also: Kwashiorkor: edema with a calorie-adequate, protein-poor diet
Nephrotic syndrome: albumin lost in urine
Cirrhosis: albumin made less

stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes omitted insulin for 3 days. He has nausea, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and glucose of 480 mg/dL with a high serum beta-hydroxybutyrate level.
oneliner: 19M + type 1 diabetes + 3 d no insulin + nausea, abdominal pain, fruity breath + glucose 480 + high beta-hydroxybutyrate → why are ketones made?
ask: Which change in the liver most directly drives ketone production?

options.A: Fatty acid oxidation rises, producing acetyl-CoA beyond what the TCA cycle can use
options.B: Depletion of pentose phosphate pathway intermediates

whyNot.B: Not involved in **ketogenesis**
whyNot.C: Fatty acid oxidation is **increased**, not blocked
whyNot.D: It is **stimulated**, which pulls oxaloacetate away
whyNot.E: Glucagon **stimulates** glycogenolysis, and glycogen is **not a ketone source**

answer: Low insulin with high glucagon: increased beta-oxidation and ketone body synthesis
why: **Insulin lack raises lipolysis and beta-oxidation**. **Oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis**, so **acetyl-CoA** cannot enter the TCA cycle and is converted to **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) via HMG-CoA.
chain: Acetyl-CoA accumulates, oxaloacetate drained to glucose

idea.rule: Ketones appear when fat oxidation outpaces the TCA cycle.
also: Prolonged starvation: same pathway without hyperglycemia
Alcoholic ketoacidosis: low carbohydrate, high NADH
Very low-carbohydrate (ketogenic) diet

stem: A 46-year-old man has bronze skin pigmentation, pain in his second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, new diabetes mellitus, and an enlarged liver. Serum ferritin is 3,200 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 85%. Hemoglobin is normal. He has had no transfusions and takes no iron supplements. A liver biopsy stained with Prussian blue is shown.
oneliner: 46M + bronze skin + 2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy + new diabetes + hepatomegaly + ferritin 3,200, TSAT 85% + no transfusions + Prussian blue liver biopsy → why iron overload?
ask: Which of the following best explains his iron overload?

options.D: Inappropriately high intestinal absorption of iron

whyNot.A: He takes **no iron supplements**; a normal diet cannot overload iron while absorption is regulated
whyNot.B: The body has **no regulated excretion route**; the problem is intake into the body
whyNot.C: Needs **ineffective erythropoiesis** (thalassemia) with anemia; his **hemoglobin is normal**
whyNot.E: He has had **no transfusions**

answer: HFE mutation with low hepcidin causes excess intestinal iron absorption
why: **HFE mutation** lowers **hepcidin**, so enterocytes and macrophages release iron freely and **absorption is inappropriately high**. Iron deposits in **liver, pancreas, heart, joints and skin**, giving cirrhosis, diabetes, arthropathy and bronzing.

idea.rule: Iron overload without transfusion = too little hepcidin effect, so absorption is too high; the body cannot excrete iron.
also: HFE C282Y homozygotes: low hepcidin
Juvenile form: hemojuvelin or hepcidin gene mutations
Ferroportin resistant to hepcidin
Non-transfused thalassemia: erythroferrone lowers hepcidin

image.prompt: Photomicrograph of liver tissue with Prussian blue stain showing abundant coarse blue granules in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes, strongest around portal tracts, with early fibrosis. Pink background. No text or labels.

stem: A 2-day-old full-term boy is lethargic and feeding poorly with vomiting and rapid breathing. Plasma ammonia is 520 µmol/L, plasma citrulline is low, BUN is low and urinary orotic acid is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 2-day-old boy + lethargy, vomiting, tachypnea + ammonia 520 + low citrulline + low BUN + high urinary orotic acid → which enzyme?
ask: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains these findings?

whyNot.A: **Orotic acid would be low**, since carbamoyl phosphate is not made
whyNot.B: Also gives **low orotic acid**, because carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is not activated
whyNot.D: Gives **high citrulline** (citrullinemia)
whyNot.E: Gives **high argininosuccinate**, with normal or high citrulline

answer: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis
why: Without **OTC**, **carbamoyl phosphate accumulates** and enters the **pyrimidine pathway**, raising **orotic acid**. **Ammonia** cannot be cleared, so **encephalopathy** develops, with **low citrulline and BUN**.
chain: Spills into pyrimidine pathway: orotic acid

idea.rule: High orotic acid with hyperammonemia and low BUN is OTC deficiency.
also: X-linked: boys hit hardest; carrier girls can decompensate with protein loads
Contrast: CPS-I and NAGS deficiency have no orotic aciduria
Contrast: UMP synthase defect has orotic aciduria with normal ammonia and megaloblastic anemia

stem: A 5-year-old boy has had very pale skin, white-blond hair and light blue-gray eyes since birth, and he squints in bright light. His parents have normal pigmentation and a brother is unaffected. A skin biopsy shows a normal number of melanocytes, but they contain no pigment.
oneliner: 5M + white-blond hair, pale skin, blue-gray eyes since birth + photophobia + normal-pigment parents + normal melanocyte count with no pigment → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains the lack of pigment?

options.A: Failed migration of melanocyte precursors from the neural crest
options.D: Dropout of melanin into the dermis
options.E: Inability of melanocytes to synthesise melanin

whyNot.A: That leaves **patches** of skin without melanocytes; here the **count is normal** and loss is uniform
whyNot.B: The biopsy shows a **normal number**
whyNot.C: Would appear **later in life** as patches, and melanocytes would be absent
whyNot.D: Gives **grey-brown patches** after inflammation, not pale skin from birth

answer: Tyrosinase deficiency (oculocutaneous albinism): melanocytes present, melanin absent
why: **Normal melanocyte number but no pigment from birth** means the cells cannot make melanin. The usual defect is **tyrosinase** (tyrosine → DOPA → melanin), inherited as an **autosomal recessive** trait, so the unaffected parents are carriers.
chain: Both alleles of the tyrosinase gene are defective
Tyrosine cannot be converted to DOPA and melanin
Sunburn, skin cancer risk and photophobia

idea.rule: Albinism: normal melanocyte count, no melanin made.
also: Piebaldism: neural crest migration defect, patches, white forelock
Vitiligo: autoimmune loss of melanocytes
Eyes: low pigment causes poor vision and nystagmus
Chediak-Higashi and Hermansky-Pudlak also have pigment problems

stem: Two people with oculocutaneous albinism, each with two mutated copies of a pigment gene, have three children. All three children have normal skin, hair and eye pigmentation.
oneliner: Couple, both with albinism (recessive) + three children all normally pigmented → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the children's phenotype?

options.D: Each parent carries mutations at a different gene locus

whyNot.A: Each parent is **fully mutant at their locus**, so no normal gamete exists at that gene
whyNot.B: One gene having **several effects**; it does not restore pigment
whyNot.C: Describes **differing severity in people who carry the genotype**, not a fully normal child
whyNot.E: Would give a child with **two mutant copies from one parent**, so affected

answer: Genetic (locus) heterogeneity: albinism genes differ between the parents
why: Albinism can result from mutations in **different genes** (TYR, OCA2 and others). Each child inherits one normal allele at **each** locus and is a **double heterozygote**, so pigmentation is normal.
chain: Parent 1 is mutant at locus A only
Parent 2 is mutant at locus B only
Child gets one normal copy of A and of B

idea.rule: Locus heterogeneity: different genes can produce the same recessive phenotype, so two affected parents can have unaffected children.
also: Same logic: some deaf couples (connexin 26 versus other genes)
Allelic heterogeneity: many mutations in one gene (CF)
Complementation is the lab test that shows two mutations are in different genes
Pedigree of two affected parents with normal children suggests locus heterogeneity

stem: A 38-year-old woman at 11 weeks has chorionic villus sampling because of her age. Both direct and cultured villus preparations show 47,XY,+15 in 30% of cells and 46,XY in the rest. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks shows 46,XY in all cells, and fetal ultrasound is normal.
oneliner: 38F + 11 wk CVS: 47,XY,+15 in 30% of cells in direct and cultured preps + amnio 46,XY + normal ultrasound → best explanation?
ask: Which of the following best explains the discordant results?

options.C: A trisomic cell line confined to the placenta
options.E: Maternal cell contamination of the villi

whyNot.A: Another patient's cells would not show the **same 46,XY line in all amniocytes**, and the trisomic line was in **both preparations**
whyNot.B: The **amniotic cells and ultrasound are normal**
whyNot.D: Found in **both direct and cultured** preparations, so not a one-colony artifact
whyNot.E: Would show **46,XX cells**, not trisomy 15 in an XY fetus

answer: Confined placental mosaicism: abnormal cell line in trophoblast only
why: CVS samples **trophoblast (placental)** cells, while amniocentesis samples **fetal** cells. A postzygotic error in the trophoblast lineage gives an **abnormal placenta and a normal fetus**. Amniocentesis resolves the question.

idea.rule: CVS reflects the placenta; amniocytes reflect the fetus.
also: Trisomy rescue in placental mosaicism can leave the fetus with UPD 15: test for Prader-Willi/Angelman
Placental trisomy may cause fetal growth restriction
Pseudomosaicism: culture artifact in a single colony
Cell-free DNA screening also reads placental DNA, so CPM causes false positives

stem: A 15-year-old girl has short stature and primary amenorrhea, with streak gonads on pelvic ultrasound. Her karyotype shows 45,X in 11 of 20 metaphase cells and 46,XX in the other 9.
oneliner: 15F + short stature + primary amenorrhea + streak gonads + karyotype 45,X in 11 cells, 46,XX in 9 → how did two cell lines arise?
ask: Which of the following best explains the two cell lines?

whyNot.A: Occurs in **meiosis** and rearranges alleles; it does not change chromosome number in some cells
whyNot.B: Describes **loss of one allele** in tumors, not a monosomy
whyNot.C: Would give an **abnormal chromosome structure**, not 45,X cells
whyNot.D: Silences an X in every cell but **does not delete a chromosome**

answer: Mosaic Turner syndrome from a postzygotic mitotic error
why: A **normal 46,XX zygote** loses an X chromosome in an early **mitotic division** (anaphase lag or nondisjunction). Daughter cells then divide into **45,X** and **46,XX lines**, a **mosaic**. Meiotic errors would put the same karyotype in all cells.
chain: One daughter cell loses an X

idea.rule: Mosaicism comes from a mitotic error after fertilization; non-mosaic aneuploidy comes from meiosis.
also: Mosaic Down syndrome: milder features
Meiotic nondisjunction instead gives the same karyotype in every cell
McCune-Albright: postzygotic GNAS mutation, patchy disease
Confined placental mosaicism: error limited to the placental lineage

stem: A 71-year-old man who lives alone has eaten mostly tea and toast for 9 months. He has bleeding gums, loose teeth and easy bruising, with painful swelling of one knee. PT, aPTT and platelet count are normal. A photograph of his lower legs is shown.
oneliner: 71M + lives alone, tea and toast 9 months + bleeding gums + loose teeth + easy bruising + painful knee + normal PT, aPTT, platelets + photo of lower legs → impaired process?
ask: Which process is impaired?

options.A: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate in clotting factors
options.D: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen

whyNot.A: Would **prolong PT**, which is normal
whyNot.B: **Ehlers-Danlos** (type VII): hypermobility and skin laxity, not diet-linked
whyNot.C: **B12 or folate** lack: megaloblastic anemia and neurologic signs, not perifollicular bleeding
whyNot.E: **Copper deficiency or Menkes**: kinky hair, infants, or anemia; not gum bleeding

answer: Vitamin C deficiency: prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate
why: **Vitamin C** keeps iron in **prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases** reduced. Without it, **collagen is poorly hydroxylated** and unstable, so **capillaries and gums are fragile**: bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhage, and normal coagulation tests.

idea.rule: Scurvy is a collagen hydroxylation defect with normal coagulation tests.
also: Vitamin C also aids iron absorption and dopamine hydroxylation
Infants on boiled milk: subperiosteal hemorrhage
Alcoholics, elderly and food-insecure patients at risk

image.prompt: Clinical photograph of an older man's bare lower legs and ankles, skin showing numerous small perifollicular hemorrhages with coiled corkscrew-shaped hairs and scattered larger purple ecchymoses. Neutral background. No text or labels.

stem: A 2-day-old boy fails newborn hearing screening in both ears, and testing shows sensorineural loss. His mother has similar deafness since childhood, and he has no cleft, no ear malformations and no renal anomaly. A photograph of the infant's head is shown.
oneliner: 2-day-old boy + bilateral sensorineural deafness + affected mother + no cleft, ear or renal anomaly + head photo shown → embryologic defect?
ask: Which embryologic process is most likely abnormal?

options.B: Neural crest cell migration and melanocyte development
options.D: Differentiation of paraxial mesoderm into somites

whyNot.A: Would cause **spina bifida or anencephaly**, not pigment and deafness
whyNot.C: Affects **vertebral and midline structures**, not melanocytes
whyNot.D: Affects **vertebrae and axial muscle**, not pigment
whyNot.E: Affects **limbs, heart and body wall**, not pigment or hearing

answer: Failure of neural crest-derived melanocytes to develop and migrate (Waardenburg syndrome)
why: **Neural crest** cells give rise to **melanocytes**. In **Waardenburg syndrome** (PAX3, MITF), melanocytes fail to reach skin, hair and the **stria vascularis of the cochlea**, giving **patchy depigmentation** (white forelock) and **sensorineural deafness**, with dominant inheritance.
chain: Neural crest melanocytes fail to migrate
No pigment in hair and iris

idea.rule: Pigment plus deafness means a neural crest melanocyte defect.
also: Neural crest also gives: adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, aorticopulmonary septum
Hirschsprung can accompany Waardenburg (type 4)
Different-colored irises and pale blue eyes also occur

image.prompt: Close-up photograph of a sleeping newborn's head and face, wearing a plain onesie, showing a distinct triangular white tuft of hair at the front hairline contrasting with otherwise dark hair. Neutral background. No text or labels.

stem: A 31-year-old man is rescued after 10 days lost in a desert with no food, drinking only water from a stream. His plasma glucose is 78 mg/dL. Glycogen stores would have been exhausted within a day or two of the start.
oneliner: 31M + 10 days without food + glucose 78 → besides liver, which organ is making glucose?
ask: Which organ, in addition to the liver, is the main site of this glucose production?

whyNot.A: Muscle **lacks glucose-6-phosphatase** and cannot release free glucose
whyNot.C: Adrenals make cortisol, which **drives** gluconeogenesis but does not perform it
whyNot.D: Pancreas makes the **hormones** (glucagon) that regulate it, not glucose
whyNot.E: The heart **consumes** fuels and has no glucose-releasing role

why: With glycogen gone, glucose is made by **gluconeogenesis**. Only the **liver and renal cortex** carry **glucose-6-phosphatase** and release free glucose, and the kidney's share rises with prolonged fasting.
chain: Glycogen runs out within about a day

idea.rule: Only tissues with glucose-6-phosphatase can release free glucose into the blood.
also: Liver (main source)
Renal cortex (more important in prolonged fasting and acidosis)
Muscle cannot, so it exports lactate and alanine for the liver to use

stem: In a metabolic study, biopsies are taken from a volunteer's quadriceps at rest and during exercise. Plasma free fatty acid levels are the same, yet fatty acid oxidation is much lower at rest. Malonyl-CoA content of the resting muscle is higher.
oneliner: Resting vs exercising muscle + same free fatty acids + less fat oxidation + higher malonyl-CoA → why?
ask: What most directly explains the lower fatty acid oxidation at rest?

options.B: Lack of carnitine in resting muscle

whyNot.A: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase **makes** malonyl-CoA; it is not what malonyl-CoA blocks
whyNot.B: Carnitine is not stated to be low; the stem points to **malonyl-CoA**
whyNot.C: Activation to fatty acyl-CoA occurs in the cytosol; the **mitochondrial entry step** is the one regulated
whyNot.E: HMG-CoA synthase is part of **ketogenesis**, not entry of fatty acids into mitochondria

why: **Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-1**, the rate-limiting step that carries fatty acyl groups into mitochondria. At rest, high energy charge keeps malonyl-CoA up, so **fatty acids cannot enter the matrix** for beta-oxidation.
chain: Resting muscle has high energy charge
Acyl groups cannot enter the mitochondria

idea.rule: Malonyl-CoA, the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, shuts off fatty acid entry into mitochondria so synthesis and oxidation do not run together.
also: Fed liver: insulin raises malonyl-CoA, so beta-oxidation is suppressed
Fasting: glucagon lowers malonyl-CoA, so CPT-1 opens and ketogenesis can proceed
Exercise: AMPK inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, malonyl-CoA falls

stem: A population survey finds a single-base difference at the same position of a gene in 30% of unrelated people. Carriers are healthy, the amino acid sequence of the protein is the same in everyone, and the variant has no effect on gene expression.
oneliner: Single-base difference in 30% of people + healthy carriers + no protein or expression change → what is it called?
ask: Which term best describes this variant?

whyNot.B: Missense **changes an amino acid**; none is changed here
whyNot.C: Nonsense **creates a stop codon**; the protein is intact
whyNot.D: Frameshift **alters the reading frame**; the protein is intact
whyNot.E: Splice-site changes **alter mRNA processing**; expression is unaffected here

why: A variant found in **more than 1% of the population** without causing disease is a **polymorphism**. It is neutral, so it persists and spreads rather than being removed by selection.
chain: It does not alter the protein or its expression
It reaches a frequency above 1% in the population

idea.rule: A common neutral DNA variant (above about 1%) is a polymorphism; a rare, harmful one is a mutation.
also: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)
Variable number tandem repeats
Blood group and HLA alleles
Restriction fragment length polymorphisms

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had three first-trimester miscarriages. Karyotyping shows that she carries an inverted chromosome segment that does not include the centromere. Her partner's karyotype is normal.
oneliner: 29F + 3 early miscarriages + inversion not including the centromere → why are her gametes unbalanced?
ask: Which event most likely produces her unbalanced gametes?

options.B: Fusion of two acrocentric long arms
options.C: Exchange of terminal segments between nonhomologous chromosomes
options.D: Loss of a centromere before S phase

whyNot.A: Nondisjunction gives **whole-chromosome** gains and losses, not an inversion effect
whyNot.B: That is a **Robertsonian translocation**, which the karyotype does not show
whyNot.C: That is a **reciprocal translocation**, not an inversion
whyNot.D: A centromere is **not lost** in this carrier; the segment is merely inverted

answer: Crossover within the inversion loop producing dicentric and acentric chromatids
why: The inverted segment must **loop** to pair with its normal homologue. A **crossover within the loop** yields **dicentric and acentric chromatids**, which give unbalanced gametes and early loss.
chain: Inverted segment forms a loop at pairing

idea.rule: Carriers of a balanced rearrangement are healthy; the harm is from unbalanced products of meiosis.
also: Pericentric inversion: crossover gives duplications and deletions
Robertsonian translocation
Reciprocal translocation

stem: In a test-tube study, purified muscle glycogen phosphorylase in its unphosphorylated form (phosphorylase b) breaks down glycogen slowly. Adding AMP raises the rate several-fold. No kinase or ATP is present in the mixture.
oneliner: Purified muscle phosphorylase b + AMP raises glycogen breakdown + no kinase or ATP → what does AMP do?
ask: What is the role of AMP in this reaction?

whyNot.A: The rate **rises**, so AMP does not inhibit
whyNot.B: Covalent modification needs a **kinase and ATP**, which are absent
whyNot.D: An inhibitor would **lower** the rate
whyNot.E: Phosphorylase kinase is **not in the mixture**

why: With **no kinase or ATP**, the enzyme cannot be phosphorylated. AMP **binds an allosteric site** of phosphorylase b and shifts it to its active conformation, signaling **low energy** in contracting muscle.
chain: Exercise lowers ATP and raises AMP
AMP binds the allosteric site of phosphorylase b
Enzyme shifts to the active form
Glycogen breakdown speeds up without phosphorylation

idea.rule: Low-energy signals such as AMP regulate enzymes allosterically, separate from hormone-driven phosphorylation.
also: AMP activates PFK-1 in glycolysis
AMP activates AMPK
ATP and glucose 6-phosphate inhibit muscle phosphorylase

stem: A 2-day-old boy has craniofacial and cardiac malformations. His mother took isotretinoin in the first trimester. Retinoic acid binds a nuclear receptor that attaches to specific DNA sequences at many chromosomal sites and changes the expression of HOX genes, so different cell types make different sets of RNAs.
oneliner: 2-day-old boy + malformations after in-utero retinoic acid + nuclear receptor binds specific DNA sites and alters HOX expression → what class of protein?
ask: Which class of protein is this receptor?

whyNot.A: A promoter is a **DNA sequence**, not a protein
whyNot.C: Translation initiation factors work on **mRNA at the ribosome**, not DNA
whyNot.D: SRP directs **ribosomes to the ER**, not gene expression
whyNot.E: The ligand is **retinoic acid itself**; the receptor is what binds it

why: A protein that **binds specific DNA sequences** and **changes which genes are expressed** is a **transcription factor**. Retinoic acid receptors and HOX proteins both act this way, so excess retinoic acid disturbs body patterning.
chain: Receptor binds response elements in DNA

idea.rule: Sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins that regulate transcription are transcription factors; they decide which RNAs a cell makes.
also: Steroid and thyroid hormone receptors
Zinc finger proteins
Homeobox (HOX) proteins
Helix-turn-helix and leucine zipper proteins

stem: A researcher treats cultured cells with a histone deacetylase inhibitor. Acetyl groups accumulate on lysine residues of histone amino-terminal tails, chromatin becomes more open, and many genes are transcribed at a higher rate.
oneliner: Histone deacetylase inhibitor + acetylated lysines on histone tails + open chromatin + more transcription → what does acetylation do?
ask: What does lysine acetylation do to histone binding to DNA?

options.A: Decreases the affinity of histones for DNA
options.B: Increases the affinity of histones for DNA
options.E: Adds negative charge to the DNA backbone

whyNot.B: Tighter binding would **compact** chromatin, the opposite of what is seen
whyNot.C: Nucleosome number is **not changed** by acetylation
whyNot.D: Methylation of CpG islands **silences** genes, the opposite
whyNot.E: The DNA backbone is **not modified** by acetylation; the histone charge is

why: Acetylation **neutralizes the positive charge** of lysine, so histones bind the **negatively charged DNA** less tightly. Chromatin relaxes into **euchromatin** and transcription rises.

idea.rule: Acetylation opens chromatin; deacetylation and DNA methylation generally silence it.
also: Inactive X chromosome: hypoacetylated histones and methylated DNA keep it silent
Imprinted alleles silenced by promoter methylation
Fragile X: CGG expansion leads to FMR1 promoter methylation and silencing

stem: A researcher clones a hen gene from genomic DNA and finds the transcribed region is 7,700 bp long, running from the cap site to the poly-A addition site. A cDNA made from mature mRNA of the same gene is only 1,872 bp. Both hybridize to the same probe.
oneliner: Genomic transcribed region 7,700 bp vs cDNA 1,872 bp, same probe → what is the extra sequence?
ask: Which sequence accounts for the extra length of the genomic clone?

whyNot.A: Exons are present in **both** the cDNA and the genomic clone
whyNot.C: Promoters lie **outside** the transcribed region described
whyNot.D: The poly-A signal is **inside the mature mRNA**, so it is in the cDNA too
whyNot.E: LTRs belong to **retroviral** DNA, not a normal hen gene

why: The gene is **transcribed with its introns**, and the **spliceosome removes them** to make mature mRNA. cDNA is copied from that mRNA, so it **lacks introns** and is much shorter than the genomic region.

idea.rule: cDNA represents only mature mRNA, so it lacks introns (and promoters and other regulatory DNA).
also: Processed pseudogenes lack introns because they arose from reverse-transcribed mRNA
Human cDNA is used to express proteins in bacteria, which cannot splice
Retroviral cDNA copies of spliced mRNA lack introns

stem: A 58-year-old woman taking tamoxifen for breast cancer has very low plasma endoxifen. Genotyping shows she is homozygous for the CYP2D6*4 allele, a recessive poor-metabolizer variant. Her parents are unrelated, and genotyping shows each carries one *4 allele and one normal allele. Her brother has never been tested.
oneliner: 58F + low endoxifen on tamoxifen + homozygous CYP2D6*4 (recessive) + both parents heterozygous + brother untested → his chance of the same genotype?
ask: What is the probability that her brother is also homozygous for CYP2D6*4?

whyNot.A: Both parents **carry *4**, so his risk is above zero
whyNot.C: 50% is his chance of being **heterozygous** (one *4 allele), not homozygous
whyNot.D: 75% is his chance of carrying **at least one** *4 allele, not two
whyNot.E: Not certain: each parent passes *4 only **half the time**

why: Both parents are **heterozygous** for *4. Each child receives the *4 allele from each parent with probability ½, so being homozygous is **½ × ½ = 25%**.
chain: Both parents each carry one *4 allele
Each child gets one allele from each parent

idea.rule: Siblings of an affected child with two healthy carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of the same recessive genotype.
also: Cystic fibrosis
Phenylketonuria
Sickle cell disease
Other autosomal recessive conditions

stem: In a liver extract, phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and glutamine are converted to 5-phosphoribosylamine. Adding the end-product nucleotides of the pathway strongly slows this first reaction.
oneliner: Liver extract + PRPP + glutamine → 5-phosphoribosylamine + end products slow it → which pathway?
ask: This reaction is the committed step of which pathway?

whyNot.A: Pyrimidine synthesis starts with **carbamoyl phosphate** and aspartate, not PRPP plus glutamine
whyNot.B: The PPP **makes** ribose 5-phosphate; it does not use PRPP and glutamine
whyNot.D: Humans **cannot synthesize folate**
whyNot.E: Heme synthesis starts with **glycine and succinyl-CoA**

why: **PRPP plus glutamine to 5-phosphoribosylamine** is the **committed step of purine synthesis**, catalyzed by PRPP amidotransferase. It is **feedback-inhibited by AMP, GMP and IMP**, the end products.

idea.rule: The committed step of a pathway is its main site of feedback inhibition by end products.
also: PFK-1 in glycolysis (inhibited by ATP and citrate)
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis
HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis
CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis (inhibited by UTP)

stem: A 45-year-old man has been fasting overnight. In his liver mitochondria, pyruvate undergoes an ATP-dependent, biotin-requiring carboxylation as the first step of glucose synthesis.
oneliner: 45M + overnight fast + hepatic mitochondrial biotin-dependent carboxylation of pyruvate → product?
ask: Which compound is the immediate product of this reaction?

whyNot.A: Made from **acetyl-CoA** by a different biotin carboxylase, not from pyruvate
whyNot.B: Made from **propionyl-CoA**, not pyruvate
whyNot.C: Pyruvate makes this by **decarboxylation**, not carboxylation
whyNot.D: Made one step **later** from oxaloacetate by PEPCK

why: **Pyruvate carboxylase** (biotin, ATP, CO2) turns pyruvate into **oxaloacetate** in the mitochondrial matrix, bypassing pyruvate kinase. PEPCK then makes phosphoenolpyruvate.
chain: Pyruvate carboxylase adds CO2 with biotin and ATP

idea.rule: Gluconeogenesis bypasses pyruvate kinase with pyruvate carboxylase, then PEPCK.
also: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin): acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin): propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA
Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase during fasting

stem: In an isotope-labeling experiment, hepatocytes make inosine monophosphate (IMP) de novo from labeled precursors. The labeled atoms are found in the purine ring at N1, N3, N9, C4, C5 and N7.
oneliner: Hepatocytes + labeled precursors → IMP purine ring labeled at N1, N3, N9, C4, C5, N7 → which amino acids donated?
ask: Which amino acids supplied atoms to the purine ring?

whyNot.A: Not used as ring donors; **none** of the three contributes
whyNot.B: Arginine and histidine are **not donors**
whyNot.C: Tyrosine gives no ring atoms, and serine feeds only **one-carbon units** (C2, C8), not the labeled atoms
whyNot.E: Glutamate, proline and serine **do not** supply the ring nitrogens

why: **Glycine** gives C4, C5 and N7, **glutamine** gives N3 and N9, and **aspartate** gives N1. CO2 and formyl-THF supply the remaining carbons.

idea.rule: Purine ring: glycine, aspartate, glutamine (plus CO2 and one-carbon units); pyrimidine ring: aspartate, glutamine, CO2.
also: Glycine: C4, C5, N7
Glutamine: N3, N9
Aspartate: N1
Formyl-THF: C2 and C8

stem: Phosphatidylcholine is incubated with a purified enzyme. Diacylglycerol appears in the lipid phase and phosphocholine in the aqueous phase. No free fatty acid or lysophospholipid is produced.
oneliner: Phosphatidylcholine + enzyme → diacylglycerol + phosphocholine, no free fatty acid → which enzyme?
ask: Which enzyme most likely catalyzed this reaction?

whyNot.A: PLA2 releases a **fatty acid and lysophospholipid**, none is seen
whyNot.B: PLD releases **choline and phosphatidic acid**, not phosphocholine and DAG
whyNot.C: Acts on **sphingomyelin**, giving ceramide
whyNot.E: A **triglyceride** lipase; it does not act on phospholipids

why: **Phospholipase C** cleaves the phosphodiester bond on the **glycerol side** of the phosphate, leaving **diacylglycerol** and releasing the phospho-headgroup. The same enzyme class cuts PIP2 into IP3 and DAG.

idea.rule: Phospholipase C removes the phospho-headgroup and leaves diacylglycerol, a second messenger.
also: PLC-beta (via Gq) cuts PIP2 into IP3 and DAG
Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that lyses membranes
PLC-gamma is activated by receptor tyrosine kinases

stem: A newly sequenced nuclear protein contains repeated 30-amino-acid motifs. Each motif folds around a zinc ion held by four cysteine residues. The protein's activity changes when a lipophilic hormone binds it.
oneliner: Nuclear protein + repeated 30-amino-acid motifs folded around Zn held by four cysteines + lipophilic hormone binding → what kind of protein?
ask: Which type of protein is this most likely to be?

whyNot.A: Ribonucleases **cut RNA** and do not need hormone binding to regulate genes
whyNot.B: DNA ligase **joins DNA strands**; no hormone control
whyNot.C: A transporter is a **membrane** protein; this one is nuclear
whyNot.D: Chaperones **assist folding**; they do not bind a hormone and act on genes

answer: Transcription factor with a zinc finger
why: Cysteines (or cysteine/histidine) **coordinating zinc** form a **zinc finger**, a DNA-binding motif. A **nuclear** protein regulated by a **lipophilic hormone** is a **transcription factor** such as a steroid receptor.
chain: Finger inserts in the DNA major groove

idea.rule: Zinc fingers are DNA-binding domains of transcription factors, including nuclear hormone receptors.
also: Glucocorticoid receptor
Estrogen receptor
Thyroid hormone receptor
Retinoic acid receptor

stem: A liver extract is supplied with glucose 6-phosphate and flux through glycolysis is measured. Output is limited by one committed step that is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP.
oneliner: Liver extract + glucose 6-phosphate → glycolytic flux limited by one step, inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP → which enzyme?
ask: Which enzyme controls the rate of this pathway?

whyNot.B: It works in **gluconeogenesis**, the reverse direction
whyNot.C: Aldolase works **near equilibrium** and is not the control point
whyNot.D: It lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, a **regulator**, not the rate-limiting enzyme
whyNot.E: It acts **before** glucose 6-phosphate, so it is not the step after the stated starting point

why: Glucose 6-phosphate is isomerized to fructose 6-phosphate, and **PFK-1** makes fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. This **committed, rate-limiting step** is **inhibited by ATP and citrate** and **activated by AMP** and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
chain: Inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP

idea.rule: Pathway flux is set by its committed, irreversible step, which carries the main allosteric controls.
also: Isocitrate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle (activated by ADP, inhibited by ATP and NADH)
Glycogen phosphorylase in glycogenolysis
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle (activated by N-acetylglutamate)
HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis

stem: A 24-year-old woman eats a large carbohydrate meal. Her insulin rises and cAMP falls in hepatocytes. Phosphofructokinase-1 activity rises sharply as it converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
oneliner: 24F + carbohydrate meal + insulin up, hepatic cAMP down + PFK-1 activity rises → which molecule is the main allosteric activator?
ask: Which molecule is the most important allosteric activator of hepatic PFK-1 here?

whyNot.A: cAMP is **low** after the meal; it promotes the opposite effect
whyNot.B: The **product** of PFK-1; it feeds forward to activate **pyruvate kinase**, not hepatic PFK-1
whyNot.C: Citrate **inhibits** PFK-1
whyNot.E: Calcium is **not** the allosteric switch for hepatic glycolysis

why: Insulin **lowers cAMP**, so the bifunctional enzyme acts as **PFK-2 (kinase)** and makes **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate**. This molecule **allosterically activates PFK-1** and so drives glycolysis.

idea.rule: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is the main hormone-linked switch of PFK-1 in liver.
also: Glucagon raises cAMP, lowers F2,6BP and favors gluconeogenesis
F2,6BP also inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase
AMP also activates PFK-1

stem: DNA from the maternal and paternal copies of chromosome 7 of one individual is digested with the same restriction enzyme and analyzed on a Southern blot with the same probe. The paternal copy gives a 10 kb band and the maternal copy a 4 kb band.
oneliner: Maternal vs paternal chromosome 7 + same enzyme and probe + 10 kb vs 4 kb bands → which phenomenon?
ask: Which term describes this difference?

whyNot.A: Chromosome walking is a **cloning technique** for neighboring sequences
whyNot.B: Segregation describes alleles **separating into gametes**; it does not explain band sizes
whyNot.C: Nondisjunction gives an **abnormal chromosome number**
whyNot.D: Recombination would **mix** the parental copies; each band here is intact

why: A **sequence variant creates or abolishes a restriction site**, so the same enzyme cuts the two alleles into **fragments of different sizes**. The probe then reveals them as separate bands.
chain: A sequence variant alters a restriction site
The same enzyme cuts each allele differently
The probe detects two distinct bands

idea.rule: Variation in restriction sites between alleles gives different fragment sizes on a Southern blot.
also: Used in early linkage analysis
Sickle cell allele detected with MstII sites
Forerunner of modern SNP genotyping

stem: An investigational drug enters cells through a channel and remains confined to the cytoplasm. It cannot cross into the nucleus, mitochondria, or endoplasmic reticulum. It directly inhibits an enzyme it contacts there.
oneliner: Drug enters cells and stays in cytosol (cannot reach nucleus, mitochondria or ER) + inhibits an enzyme it contacts → which process is affected?
ask: Which process is most directly affected?

whyNot.A: Occurs in the **nucleus**, which the drug cannot enter
whyNot.B: Occurs on the **inner mitochondrial membrane**
whyNot.D: Secreted proteins fold in the **ER lumen**
whyNot.E: Occurs in the **mitochondrial matrix**

why: The drug can only reach **cytosolic** enzymes. **Glycolysis** takes place in the cytosol, while transcription, electron transport, ER folding and beta-oxidation are in other compartments.
chain: Drug is restricted to the cytosol
Nuclear and mitochondrial pathways are out of reach
ER pathways are out of reach
Cytosolic glycolysis enzymes are directly affected

idea.rule: Match where a drug is located to the pathways compartmentalized there.
also: Cytosol: glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis, pentose phosphate pathway
Mitochondria: TCA cycle, beta-oxidation, electron transport
Both: gluconeogenesis, urea cycle, heme synthesis

stem: Isolated liver mitochondria are incubated in a medium without carnitine, each with a different oxidizable substrate. Oxygen consumption rises with all of them except one.
oneliner: Isolated liver mitochondria + no carnitine + one substrate not oxidized → which one?
ask: Which substrate cannot be oxidized under these conditions?

whyNot.B: Crosses the inner membrane via a **pyruvate carrier**, no carnitine needed
whyNot.C: Enters by the **dicarboxylate carrier** and is oxidized by complex II; no carnitine
whyNot.D: A **medium-chain** fatty acid that crosses freely
whyNot.E: Taken up by a **carrier** and metabolized in the matrix

why: **Long-chain** fatty acids like palmitate are made into palmitoyl-CoA in the cytosol, and **cannot cross the inner membrane without carnitine** (CPT-I, translocase, CPT-II). Without it, they cannot be oxidized.
chain: Palmitate activated to palmitoyl-CoA in the cytosol
Translocase moves it into the matrix

idea.rule: Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane without carnitine.
also: Medium-chain fatty acids enter without carnitine
Carnitine deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia
CPT-II deficiency causes exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis

stem: A 9-year-old girl has a rhabdomyosarcoma. Her father and paternal aunt had sarcomas and early breast cancer, and she carries a germline TP53 mutation. Her skin fibroblasts and normal control fibroblasts are irradiated in culture. Flow cytometry 24 hours later shows the control cells piled up with unreplicated (2N) DNA content, while her cells carry on to 4N.
oneliner: 9F + rhabdomyosarcoma + family sarcomas and early breast cancer + germline TP53 variant + irradiated fibroblasts fail to stop cycling → where do normal cells arrest?
ask: At which transition do the control cells normally arrest?

whyNot.A: Arrest here would pile cells up with **4N** DNA; the controls stay at **2N**
whyNot.C: The spindle checkpoint holds cells in **mitosis**, after DNA is already replicated
whyNot.D: Cells would show **intermediate (2N to 4N)** DNA content, not 2N
whyNot.E: Occurs **after** division; it is not a DNA-damage checkpoint

answer: Arrest at the G1/S transition, which needs functional p53
why: After DNA damage, **p53** is stabilised and induces **p21**, which blocks cyclin E-CDK2 so **Rb stays unphosphorylated** and cells are held before S phase. Her mutant p53 cannot do this, so damaged DNA is replicated.
chain: Rb stays hypophosphorylated, cells held at G1/S

idea.rule: p53 is the guardian of the G1/S checkpoint: it pauses cells to repair DNA or sends them to apoptosis.
also: Germline TP53 loss: Li-Fraumeni syndrome
HPV E6 protein degrades p53
MDM2 overexpression inactivates p53
TP53-mutant tumours resist radiation (no G1 arrest or apoptosis)

stem: A 16-year-old girl is tall with long fingers and an arm span greater than her height. FBN1 sequencing shows a single-base change that leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged. Her unaffected mother carries the same change, and it is found in 15 of 200 healthy controls.
oneliner: 16F + tall, long fingers + FBN1 change with same amino acid + unaffected mother has it + 15 of 200 controls → how to classify the variant?
ask: How is this FBN1 change best classified?

whyNot.A: A disease-causing change would **not** be carried by an **unaffected** mother or seen in 7.5% of controls
whyNot.B: Reserved for **rare** changes without data; this one is **common in controls**
whyNot.C: The **amino acid is unchanged**, so there is no premature stop
whyNot.E: It is **inherited** from her mother

why: A variant present in **more than 1%** of healthy people is a **polymorphism**. Being silent (**same amino acid**) and shared by an unaffected relative fits a harmless variant, so it does not explain her features.
chain: Found in more than 1% of controls and in unaffected mother
Classified as a polymorphism, not the cause

idea.rule: A variant found in more than 1% of the healthy population is a polymorphism, not a disease-causing mutation.
also: Most single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)
ABO blood group alleles
HLA alleles
Common synonymous variants seen in healthy relatives

stem: A 24-year-old man has eaten nothing since dinner. At 7 AM, 11 hours later, his blood glucose is 82 mg/dL, insulin is low, glucagon is high, and urine ketones are negative.
oneliner: 24M + no food for 11 h + glucose 82 + insulin low, glucagon high + urine ketones negative → main source of blood glucose?
ask: Which process is mainly maintaining his blood glucose now?

whyNot.B: Already running, but becomes the **main** source only **after about 24 hours**, once glycogen is used up
whyNot.C: Minor contributor early on; major only in **prolonged** fasting
whyNot.D: Muscle lacks **glucose-6-phosphatase** and cannot release glucose
whyNot.E: Ketones are **negative**; this does not supply blood glucose

why: In the first **6 to 24 hours** after a meal the liver breaks down its glycogen stores, driven by **low insulin and high glucagon**, and releases glucose. **Gluconeogenesis** dominates once glycogen runs out after about a day.

idea.rule: Fasting fuel order: liver glycogen first (hours), then gluconeogenesis, then ketones.
also: Overnight fast: liver glycogen supplies most glucose
Glucagon and epinephrine activate glycogen phosphorylase (cAMP-PKA)
Fasting beyond 1 day: gluconeogenesis from amino acids, lactate, glycerol
Prolonged starvation: brain switches to ketones

stem: In a culture of oviduct epithelium, estrogen exposure makes many cells form hundreds of new cilia each. The cells do not divide. Electron microscopy shows rows of basal bodies appearing below the apical membrane before the cilia grow.
oneliner: Oviduct epithelium culture + estrogen + hundreds of new cilia per cell + no cell division + basal bodies first → required process?
ask: Which process is required for this ciliogenesis?

whyNot.B: Mitochondria **power** cilia but do not **form** the basal bodies
whyNot.C: Cytokeratin is an **intermediate filament**, not part of the axoneme
whyNot.E: Smooth ER is not involved in **basal body** formation
whyNot.D: The cells are **not dividing**; DNA content is unchanged

why: Each cilium grows from a **basal body**, a modified **centriole**. The cell makes **many new centrioles**, which move to the apical surface and nucleate the axonemal microtubules.
chain: Migrate to apical surface as basal bodies

idea.rule: Every cilium or flagellum grows from a basal body, which is derived from a centriole.
also: Sperm flagellum grows from the distal centriole
The primary cilium of most cells grows from the mother centriole
Multiciliated airway cells amplify centrioles the same way
